short: Classical dance and music in India
title: Classical Dance and Music in India: Where to Watch and Learn
seoTitle: Classical Dance & Music in India: Where to See Them | Kudozz Club
metaDescription: India's classical dance and music for travellers: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Odissi and more, the Chennai music season, dance festivals and where to watch.
description: A traveller's guide to India's classical dance and music: the classical dance forms recognised by the Sangeet Natak Akademi, Hindustani and Carnatic music, folk forms such as Kalbelia, Chhau and Garba, and where to watch them, from Kathakali in Kochi and the Chennai music season to the Khajuraho and Konark dance festivals.
dek: India's classical dance and music are living traditions, performed in temples, festivals and small halls as well as big stages. Here is how to see them on your travels.
intro: India has two great classical music traditions, Hindustani in the north and Carnatic in the south, and several classical dance forms, each linked to a region. The Sangeet Natak Akademi, India's national academy for music and dance, recognises eight classical dances; the Ministry of Culture's list also includes Chhau.
Alongside them are hundreds of folk and ritual forms. UNESCO has inscribed several on its Intangible Cultural Heritage lists, including Kutiyattam, Chhau, Kalbelia and Garba.
quickAnswer: India's classical dances include Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (north India), Kathakali and Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur) and Sattriya (Assam). Travellers can watch Kathakali in Kochi most evenings, the Chennai music season in December and January, and winter dance festivals at Khajuraho, Konark and Mamallapuram.
takeaways: The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises eight classical dance forms.
Kathakali performances for visitors run most evenings in Kochi; arrive early to watch the make-up.
The Chennai music season runs from about mid-December to mid-January.
Winter brings dance festivals to Khajuraho, Konark and Mamallapuram; dates vary each year.
Kalbelia, Chhau, Garba and Kutiyattam are on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage lists.

sections.heading: Hindustani and Carnatic music
paras: Hindustani music, from the north, is built around ragas developed at length, often with sitar, sarod, tabla or voice. Carnatic music, from the south, is more composition-based, with voice, veena, violin and mridangam. Both are best heard live, in concert halls, temples and festivals, and many concerts are free or inexpensive.

items.name: Chennai music season
body: From about mid-December to mid-January, the city's sabhas host hundreds of concerts and dance recitals.

items.name: Kathakali in Kochi
body: Short performances for visitors are held most evenings in Fort Kochi and Ernakulam, often with a make-up session beforehand.

items.name: Winter dance festivals
body: The Khajuraho Dance Festival (usually February), the Konark Dance Festival (December) and the Mamallapuram Dance Festival (December to January), staged with monuments as the backdrop.

items.name: Music festivals
body: The Tansen Samaroh in Gwalior and the Sawai Gandharva festival in Pune, both usually in December.

sections.heading: Etiquette at performances
list: Arrive early; late entry during a piece is frowned upon.
Ask before photographing; flash is usually not allowed.
At ritual performances such as Theyyam, you are a guest at worship; follow local guidance.
Silence phones, and stay until the end of a piece before leaving.

sections.heading: Learning a little first
paras: A little knowledge makes a big difference. Most classical dances combine pure dance (nritta), expressive storytelling (abhinaya) and drama (natya). Stories often come from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata, the Puranas or devotional poetry. At a Kathakali performance, the colour of the make-up signals the character: green for noble heroes, red and black for villains. Many visitor shows explain the hand gestures (mudras) before they begin.

faqs.a: No, but it helps; read a short synopsis or ask for one, and watch the hand gestures and facial expressions that carry the story.
